course_details.Overview of class: Students in Beginning German 101-2 will continue to expand their active vocabulary in German, improve their understanding of grammatical concepts and further their oral and aural comprehension skills. Students will be able to interview a guest in German and write a biographical essay by the end of the quarter. Features of 101-2 include varied writing assignments, cultural presentations, poems by Goethe, as well as an interview with a native speaker or "Mystery Guest" that will form the basis for the final essay.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
The following Can-Do statements define the course expectations and learning objectives. Here is what you can expect to be able to accomplish in this course:

Understanding: Listening: I can recognize high frequency vocabulary and basic phrases concerning myself, my family and immediate concrete surroundings when people speak slowly and clearly.

Reading: I can read very short, simple texts. I can find specific, predictable information in simple everyday material such as advertisements, prospectuses, menus and timetables and I can understand short simple personal letters.

Speaking: Spoken Interaction: I can interact in a simple way provided the other person is prepared to repeat or rephrase things at a slower rate of speech and help me formulate what I'm trying to say. I can ask and answer simple questions in areas of immediate need or on very familiar topics.

Spoken Production: I can use a series of phrases and sentences to describe in simple terms my family and other people, living conditions, my educational background and my present or most recent job.

Writing: Writing: I can write a short, simple postcard. I can fill in forms with personal details, for example entering my name, nationality and address on a hotel registration form. I can write short, simple notes and messages relating to matters in areas of immediate needs. I can write a very simple personal letter or describe personal routines and plans.

course_details.Overview of class: Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834) was one of the most important writers and thinkers of his time. His innovations include the organization of the modern research university, his theory of the self, and his understanding of religion. We focus our attention in this course to his work from 1799, On Religion: Speeches to its Cultured Despisers, as we discuss how this foundational text in the study of religion is also a literary treasure, a model for the relation of religion to the state, and how religion is central to both self and community. Please purchase required text, translated by Richard Crouter with ISBN 978-0521479752, published by Cambridge University Press 1996 ($56) well in advance of the first day of class.
course_details.Registration Requirements: This a first-year seminar in the Weinberg College
course_details.Learning Objectives:
To read a classic of German literature on religion as an entire book and with understanding.
To know the basic argument of the book and its constituent steps.
To appreciate the genre and rhetoric of the speeches.
To write a paper that is coherent, well argued, judiciously documented, and written in clear prose.

course_details.Overview of class: The class will provide an introduction to the period of the German Empire or Kaiserreich 1871 - 1918. It examines the explosion of art and industry at the turn of the century that for the first time included substantial opportunities for women. This epoch in German history is emblematic for modernism. Through short historical texts, biographies, letters and journals, students will learn about social issues, German politics and art movements. Historical figures of the period included Bismarck, Kaiser Wilhelm II, and Käthe Kollwitz. Visits to the Art Institut, the Block Museum and the Milwaukee Art Museum are planned. Students will complete a project-based presentation and paper in lieu of a final exam.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Students should have completed their language requirement with 102-3, have German AP score of 4, or permission of the DUS.
course_details.Learning Objectives: The course serves as a bridge course to more advanced culture and literature courses in the German department. It provides an opportunity for students to work intensively on their reading and comprehension skills but also has a strong communicative component, as the readings will provide the basis for interpretive discussions, short presentations and written work.

course_details.Overview of class: This class considers the history and culture of Berlin from 1900 to the present. Through a wide range of media (literature, film, photography, historical documents) we can see a series of transformative moments in German cultural history through the prism of Berlin. Students will engage with the varied historical, socio-political, and artistic changes in German culture throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, including: the vibrant and provocative culture of the 1920s and early 1930s, with a focus on changing forms of gender identity (the "New Woman") and sexual and political subcultures; the everyday and extraordinary history of German-Jews in Germany both before and after the Jewish genocide carried out by the Nazi regime;. the devastated city of postwar Berlin, the city's subsequent division during the Cold War (including the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961. In the final weeks we consider the momentous fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the creation of the Berlin Republic. We will familiarize ourselves with the changing face of national culture in light of the migration of the so-called Turkish "guest workers" from the post-War years and the subsequent emergence of Berlin a a global city. This course highlights the ways in which cosmopolitan Berlin remains a magnetic international destination with a biography and personality all its own.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Explore and evaluate twentieth-century German (central European) history, beginning with the years immediately preceding WWI and ending with contemporary Berlin
• Analyze shifting representations of gender and sexuality in the urban context of twentieth-century Berlin
• Articulate a critical approach to the history of minority communities in Berlin, especially through examining Jewish- and Turkish-German culture
• Define broad tendencies and changes in literary and film culture from the turn of the twentieth century to recent postmodernism
• Experience and evaluate the changing media landscape with the development of modern technologies of reproduction via visual art, sound recordings, and films associated with Berlin

1880 Campus Drive, Kresge, Office 3325
Office Hours: Wednesdays 2-3:30 and by appointment
course_details.Overview of class: This course examines Prague, one of the most beautiful and culturally vibrant cities in Europe. The city's magnificent streets and buildings both conceal and reveal a past full of multiethnic coexistence and interethnic conflict. The course follows the development of Prague over the past century from the interwar multicultural, democratic city to the postwar homogeneous, communist community, and ultimately to its present open and capitalist incarnation. The goal of our course will be to understand how Prague's various communities built the city and its culture(s) and how they struggled to control it. We will read and watch a range of literary and historical sources, including the story of the Golem and writings by Václav Havel, and Franz Kafka.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
- To consider the productive (as well as the destructive) consequences of interethnic strife and political repression
- To investigate how cultural producers and consumers respond to divisive pressures from within and censorious pressures from without.
- To understand the contingent and malleable nature of national and other identities.
- To gain familiarity with the city of Prague and its culture

course_details.Overview of class: This course explores the central place the concept of "religion" has occupied in the development of critical theory and, in turn, the role critical theory has played in reframing "religion" in modernity and in the contemporary geopolitical moment. We take up questions of politics and capitalism in relation to religion, and we consider the contributions of "religion" to possibilities of social transformation. Readings by: Schleiermacher, Kierkegaard, Schmitt, Strauss, Fraser, Jaeggi, Saito, Gibson-Graham, Helmer, and Mariña.
course_details.Registration Requirements: This is a graduate seminar. Upper-level undergraduates only with permission of instructor.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
"To read and discuss with understanding significant texts in the contemporary discussion of critical theory, religion, and capitalism.
To write three short papers that demonstrate critical and constructive analysis of the readings."

course_details.Overview of class: This course provides an introduction to foundational texts in the history of modern western (primarily German) theoretical aesthetics. Starting from Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten's emphatic appropriation the term "aesthetics" to designate the study of beauty and good taste, the course will move chronologically through major texts of aesthetic theory from the eighteenth to the twenty-first century. The course will simultaneously examine the specific problems and questions raised by the course texts and consider the texts as historical documents, looking at the ways in which they both respond to one another and to the political and cultural tensions of their respective eras. We will also consider the ways in which these texts cross disciplinary boundaries or indeed are always already transdisciplinary, constantly moving from the fields of artistic and literary criticism to fundamental issues of ethics, epistemology, politics, and psychology and back again, always asking ourselves the questions: What are the historical and political conditions of the ways in which we make and/or think about works of art, broadly conceived, and how do these historical and political conditions, in turn, shape the world that art is said to reflect?
course_details.Registration Requirements: Graduate students (advanced undergraduates with instructor permission)
course_details.Learning Objectives:
- To learn about the history and background of modern western aesthetics in its historical, social, and philosophical contexts
- To be able to draw on this background in relation to individual works of art, literature, and culture
- To gain skills in analyzing and discussing theoretical and philosophical texts on a professional level
